analysis.one_liner: Expands Social Security benefits and pays for it by lifting the payroll tax cap on high earners.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees in May 2019 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise Social Security benefits for retirees, disabled workers, and surviving spouses, and make annual cost-of-living adjustments track what seniors actually buy. To pay for it, it would gradually eliminate the cap that stops Social Security payroll taxes on wages above about $132,900, so that by 2025 every dollar of wages would be taxed. It also protects low-income SSI recipients from benefit changes.
analysis.who_benefits: Retirees, disabled workers, and widows and widowers would get higher monthly benefits and slightly larger annual inflation adjustments. Survivors in two-income households who now get reduced benefits would see them raised. People receiving Supplemental Security Income would be held harmless from the changes.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors, disabled workers, and surviving spouses

how_it_helps.text: The benefit formula is made more generous: the first benefit tier would count 95 percent of average earnings instead of 90 percent, and the dollar threshold of that tier would grow 1 percentage point each year starting in 2025, reaching 15 percent above today's formula by 2040.

Workers' earnings above the current taxable cap would begin counting toward their benefit, adding 5 percent of such 'surplus' earnings to their benefit calculation, so the people paying the new tax also earn higher benefits.
Annual cost-of-living adjustments would be computed using a new Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, which tracks the spending patterns of retirees rather than the general population.
Widows and widowers in two-income households, who under current law often receive only a fraction of the couple's combined benefits, would be guaranteed a higher surviving-spouse benefit.
Supplemental Security Income recipients would be protected: their Social Security income would be counted as if the benefit expansions had not happened, so they would not lose SSI eligibility.
The new payroll tax would phase in over four years, so wages above the cap would be 20 percent taxable in 2021, 60 percent in 2023, and fully taxable by 2025.

analysis.who_pays: High earners — roughly the top slice of workers making more than about $132,900 — and their employers, who together would pay up to the full 12.4 percent Social Security tax on every dollar of wages once the cap is fully phased out in 2025.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners above the wage cap and their employers

drawbacks.text: The tax falls on a small group: workers and self-employed people with wages above the cap would pay substantially more in payroll tax, and their employers would pay a matching share, which could pressure hiring or pay at the top of the wage scale.

Critics of this approach have long argued that taxing above the cap while also paying benefits on that same income recaptures part of the revenue in higher benefits, so the bill improves solvency less than a cap change alone would; the bill itself contains no full actuarial solvency plan.

The faster, senior-specific cost-of-living index and the richer benefit formula raise long-term program costs that the payroll tax change may not fully offset, pushing some of the financing question to future Congresses.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is real and targeted: a more generous formula for new and existing beneficiaries, an inflation index that matches what seniors buy, and a fix for underpaid survivors, with low-income SSI recipients protected. The cost falls on a small, high-income group through a payroll tax that phases in over four years and partially pays for itself in higher benefits for those same earners. The main honest objection is on financing: counting high earnings toward benefits means the bill strengthens Social Security but does not by itself guarantee permanent solvency.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Ways and Means and Education and Labor committees the day it was introduced, and neither committee ever acted on it, so it died when the two-year Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Linda Sánchez introduced the bill on May 9, 2019, joined by 16 Democratic cosponsors.
The same day, it was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and the Education and Labor Committee, which is standard for bills spanning tax and benefit law.
No committee hearing, markup, floor vote, or further action of any kind followed before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners above the payroll tax cap and their employers are better off, since they never faced the new tax. Social Security beneficiaries are no better off, because the benefit expansions never happened.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners above the wage cap and their employers

for.name: Rep. Linda T. Sánchez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 16 Democratic cosponsors on the day of introduction.

for.name: 16 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no cosponsor added afterward.

against.name: Rep. Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it untouched in committee for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Speaker Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor; it never advanced past committee referral.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat — 17 of the 231 House Democrats in all — and no Republican supported the bill; the House leadership, also Democratic, never moved it.

industries.industry: High earners and high-wage businesses (employers of workers above the wage cap)
industries.note: Once the cap is phased out, every dollar of wages above roughly $132,900 would face the combined 12.4 percent Social Security tax, split between the worker and the employer. The cost falls on a small, high-income slice of households and on firms that employ them, which is the bill's chosen way to fund broader benefits.

Beneficiaries would receive richer benefit formulas and a cost-of-living index built around retiree spending. This is a constituency of ordinary people rather than an industry, and it was the bill's direct beneficiary.
